1.pericope_label: The death and burial of Samuel, and David’s withdrawal to the wilderness of Paran

schools.summary: Ellicott holds that since Moses none so great as Samuel had arisen, and recapitulates the work: his influence restored the Law of Moses to the affections of a people who had almost forgotten the lawgiver’s words and were becoming hardly distinguishable from the tribes around them; he taught the down-trodden Israelites that they were the chosen of God; and by creating a monarchy he welded the twelve divisions into one, from Dan to Beersheba one chief and one standard. His greatest work, Ellicott insists, was founding the prophetic schools, where men were trained to become in their turn the teachers of the people. He dates the death about the time Saul and David met at En-gedi, fastens through Stanley on the emphasis that ALL the Israelites, not one fragment only as might have been expected in a time of division, were gathered round him who had been the father of all alike, and agrees the burial place must be the court or garden, since burying him indoors would have occasioned perpetual ceremonial defilement. Of the wilderness he reports that the Septuagint reads Maon for Paran, its translators doubting David’s camp lay so far from the scene of what follows, but holds the emendation unnecessary, since Paran seems to have given its name to the whole barren tract of which the wilderness of Judah would form part.

Henry dwells on the obscurity of Samuel’s last years, which was not senility, since he still knew how to preside in a college of the prophets, but the consequence of Israel having rejected him and of his own desire to be quiet; let old people be willing to rest, he adds, though it look like burying themselves alive. The nation had reason to mourn, for they had all a loss in him: the sons of the prophets had lost the founder of their college, and Samuel was a constant intercessor who prayed daily for Israel, so in losing him they parted with the best friend they had, and there was never more need of him than at that juncture. Those have hard hearts, Henry says, who bury their faithful ministers with dry eyes. He notes the burial was not at Naioth among the prophets but in Samuel’s own house, or its garden, at Ramah where he was born; and he reads David’s move as fear rather than geography, since having lost so good a friend he thought his danger greater than ever and withdrew beyond the limits of Israel.

Gill weighs the Jewish authorities on the date, some making it four months before Saul and some seven, while Abarbinel thinks a year or two, which Gill calls most likely and indeed certain, since David was afterwards in Philistine country a full year and four months and Saul was not then dead; and the Jews fix the day as the twentieth of Ijar, for which a fast was kept.

Clarke handles the same chronological material and refuses the conclusion: Samuel lived about ninety-eight years and governed Israel before Saul for sixteen to twenty, and though the Jews say four months and Calmet two years, all this is very uncertain, and how long he died before Saul cannot be ascertained. Of the burial he thinks it means not the dwelling-house but the tomb Samuel had made for his sepulture, as the Syriac and Arabic seem to have understood it; and he places Paran on the confines of Judea or in Arabia Petraea between the mountains of Judah and Sinai, arguing from the history that it cannot have been far from Carmel.

debates.question: How long before Saul did Samuel die?

positions.view: A year or two, with Abarbinel; and this is not merely likely but certain from the later chronology
It cannot be ascertained; the Jewish four months and Calmet’s two years are both very uncertain

debates.question: Where was the wilderness David withdrew to?

positions.view: Paran, on the confines of Judea or in Arabia Petraea, but not far from Carmel
Paran as the name of the whole barren tract, of which the wilderness of Judah formed part; the Septuagint’s Maon is an unnecessary emendation

outliers.claim: Alone in giving a full account of Samuel’s achievement — the recovery of the Law, the welding of the tribes, and above all the prophetic schools — rather than only of his death.
Alone in concluding that the date simply cannot be established, against the confidence of the Jewish chronologers he reports.

themes: And Samuel died; and all the Israelites were gathered together, and lamented him
and buried him in his house at Ramah
And David arose, and went down to the wilderness of Paran

2.pericope_label: Nabal and Abigail introduced, David’s ten young men sent to Carmel, and the churlish refusal

schools.summary: Ellicott sets out the apparatus of the name: the word means fool, from a root meaning to fade away, and was probably a nickname for his stubborn folly; of the descent the Hebrew reads Kalibi, of the house of Caleb, an alternative pointing gives according to his heart, and Josephus and the Septuagint with the Arabic and Syriac derive it from the word for dog and render him a cynical man, while the Chaldee and Vulgate follow the received text, which Ellicott judges preferable. He makes the Carmel the small town and not the famous mountain, calls Abigail, with Stanley, the good angel of an ill-starred and boorish chieftain’s household, and reads David’s position as resembling a modern Arab sheik’s, his career as head of an army of free lances tending to popularise him among the southern tribes, so that the shepherds’ testimony may be taken as the popular estimate of him in this period. Keil and Delitzsch place Maon in the mountains of Judah and insist the Carmel here is the present Kurmul, scarcely half an hour north-west of it; of the obscure greeting they admit it was handled by the early translators merely by conjecture, the simplest explanation being long life; and of the refusal they say that to justify his covetousness Nabal set David down as a vagrant run from his master.

Clarke reports the Greek rendering, a doggish man, and derives the Latin nebulo, a knave, from this Hebrew root. He presses David’s claim as a debt: David not only did the herdmen no hurt and took none of their flocks, but protected them from the rapacity of others, so that they were a wall unto us by night and day, where wandering hordes think they may exact provisions at will; and he judges the refusal unjust, the request having been reasonable and modest. Wesley adds a triple obligation: considering the licentiousness of soldiers and the necessities David was under, the forbearance was no small favour, which Nabal was bound in justice and gratitude and prudence to requite; and he reads the greeting as double-edged, congratulating Nabal’s felicity while tacitly minding him of the distress David was in.

Henry takes the descent as the sting: Nabal inherited Caleb’s estate, Maon and Carmel lying near Hebron, but not his virtues, and a good extraction is a reproach to the man who degenerates from it. Of the pairing he makes a maxim, that riches are common blessings which God often gives to Nabals, to whom he gives neither wisdom nor grace, and many an Abigail is tied to a Nabal. He notes David chose a good time, when many hands were employed in shearing and good cheer was stirring, so that Nabal could not pretend he had nothing to spare; and of the greeting he accepts our translators’ addition, in prosperity, but turns it against the man, since those who live in pleasure are dead while they live, calling it too high a compliment for such a muck-worm, for which David was well served by the rough answer.

Gill reports Ben Gersom’s reading of Maon as a dwelling place, noted to show that Nabal lived not in a city but where his business lay, and Kimchi’s view that the name was a nickname men gave him to suit his genius and conduct. Of the obscure greeting he offers a reading no one else gives, taking it as a wish for the year to come: thus may it be for life, so that at the next shearing Nabal may be in as great prosperity as now. Of the refusal he says Nabal answered in great wrath, as covetous persons do when they will not give.

debates.question: Was Nabal of the house of Caleb, or a dog-like man?

positions.view: Of the house of Caleb, following the received Hebrew with the Chaldee and Vulgate; the preferable meaning
The Greek and the Syriac and Arabic read a doggish man, from the word for dog
Of Caleb, and that is the reproach: he had the estate without the virtues

debates.question: How should the obscure word in the greeting be rendered?

positions.view: Long life, a wish meaning good fortune to you; the early translators had only conjecture
A wish for the coming year: that at the next shearing he may be as prosperous as now
In prosperity, as our translators add — but the compliment was too high for such a man

outliers.claim: Alone in reading David’s band sociologically, as a sheik’s following whose protection of the border made him popular, and the shepherds’ evidence as the popular estimate of him.
Alone in rendering the greeting as a wish for the next year’s prosperity rather than as a form of address.

themes: the name of the man was Nabal; and the name of his wife Abigail: and she was a woman of good understanding
the man was churlish and evil in his doings; and he was of the house of Caleb
thy shepherds which were with us, we hurt them not, neither was there ought missing unto them
Who is David? and who is the son of Jesse?
Shall I then take my bread, and my water, and my flesh that I have killed for my shearers?

12.pericope_label: The messengers return, David arms four hundred men, and a servant warns Abigail

schools.summary: Henry commends the messengers for breaking off abruptly from such a churl and yet governing themselves so well as not to render railing for railing, nor to take by force what ought of right to have been given, leaving David to do as he thought fit. He supplies the words of David’s complaint, that surely in vain had he kept all that this fellow had in the wilderness, since the man had requited him evil for good, and answers it with the rule that when we are so requited we should not repent of the good we have done, for God is kind to the evil and unthankful. His verdict on the resolution is the most unsparing in the chapter: it was bloody, to cut off all the males of Nabal’s house and spare neither man nor man-child, and the oath that ratified it was passionate; is this thy voice, O David, he asks, and can the man after God’s own heart speak thus unadvisedly with his lips, when he who used to be dumb under reproach and had just spared the man who sought his life will now spare nothing belonging to one who has merely affronted his messengers. He alone explains why the affront found David unguarded: from Saul he expected injuries and was prepared for them and kept his temper, but from Nabal he expected kindness, so the affront was a surprise.

Keil and Delitzsch report the muster exactly and the motive candidly: the churlish reply could not fail to excite his anger, so he commanded his people to gird on the sword and started with four hundred men to take vengeance, two hundred remaining with the baggage. They then judge that however intelligible the wrath may appear in the situation he was in, it was not right before God but a sudden burst of sinful passion, unseemly in a servant of God, and that by carrying out his intention he would have sinned against the Lord and against his people, from which the Lord preserved him by Abigail hearing of it just at the right time. Ellicott reads the formality of the preparation and the size of the force as evidence of how terribly David was in earnest and how bent on wiping out the insult in blood, and condenses the verdict into the phrase that the anger is quite to be accounted for though not to be excused. He weighs the young man’s speech to Abigail as evidence from someone in high authority on the farms, clear and decisive, bearing weighty witness in the heart of an episode most discreditable to David to the admirable discipline and kind forethought of the son of Jesse, since few men could have moulded a wild company of free lances into a force that was positively a blessing to the country rather than, as such bands usually are, a curse; he takes Abigail to have often acted as peace-maker between her intemperate husband and his neighbours and to have seen at once, with a clever woman’s wit, what consequences must follow; and he notes that Belial is no proper name but signifies simply worthlessness.

Gill reads the messengers’ restraint as judgement rather than meekness: they turned their backs without reply and treated Nabal with silent contempt, but were determined to report the usage to David, who they doubted not would avenge the affront. Of the shepherds’ testimony he specifies what the protection amounted to, a wall by night and day against the Philistines, the plundering Arabs of the wilderness, and the wild beasts.

debates.question: Was the messengers’ silence before Nabal meekness or contempt?

positions.view: Self-government: they did not render railing for railing, nor take by force what should have been given
Silent contempt, with a settled intention of having the affront avenged

outliers.claim: Alone in accounting for the loss of temper by the direction the injury came from: injuries from Saul were expected and guarded against, kindness from Nabal was expected and the affront came as a surprise.
Alone in treating the servant’s report as independent testimony to David’s discipline over his men, set deliberately against the discredit of the surrounding narrative.

themes: So David’s young men turned their way, and went again, and came and told him all those sayings
Gird ye on every man his sword
and about four hundred men went up after David; and two hundred abode by the stuff
he is such a son of Belial, that one cannot speak to him
they were a wall unto us both by night and day

18.pericope_label: Abigail’s present, her ride to meet David, and the oath David had sworn

schools.summary: Ellicott reports the versions’ discomfort with the quantity, the Septuagint altering the measure of grain to five ephahs because the amount seemed ridiculously small for such a host and Ewald proposing to change five to five hundred, and holds the received text on the ground that Abigail in haste provided a liberal present for David’s immediate followers rather than for the whole force. He treats the two verses recalling David’s words as a parenthesis expressing what David felt and his justification in his own mind, that Nabal had returned evil for good, the band having long guarded his scattered flocks, and that when a small favour was asked the churl threw in his teeth the taunt of a rebel and a runaway slave. Of the oath he calls the form an unusual variation, notes that the Syriac and Arabic read his servant David where the received text has the enemies of David and that the Septuagint cuts the knot by dropping the difficult word, but keeps the Hebrew and takes the words to signify David himself. Keil and Delitzsch itemise the present without comment, reckoning the roasted grain at an ephah and two-thirds, observe that she sent the gifts on before and followed behind in order to appease his anger by meeting him in a friendly manner, without a word to Nabal of what she intended, and gloss the place of meeting as probably a hollow between two peaks, which explains why the text says both parties came down, Abigail approaching from one side and David from the other; Ellicott adopts that explanation.

Clarke treats the present as ample and the original request as modest, explaining that Eastern bread is thin and small, answering to our cakes, and that the bottles are goat-skins with the hide pulled off without ripping up and the leg-holes sewn so that the skin becomes one large bag, and reckoning that out of three thousand sheep Nabal could not have missed five, the claim coming only at shearing, which was a small price for such services. On David’s oath he passes judgement without qualifying it: nothing can justify this part of his conduct, for whatever the provocation he had suffered no wrong, and the resolution to cut off a whole innocent family was abominable and cruel, not to say diabolic, so that whoever attempts to vindicate it is at least constructively a foe to God and truth. Wesley defends Abigail’s acting without her husband from necessity: the case was one of apparent necessity, and surely the necessity that dispenses with God’s positive commands might dispense with the husband’s right.

Henry praises both the speed and the agency, since it was no time to trifle when all was in danger and, being a woman of great prudence, she knew better how to manage it than any servant could, the virtuous woman looking well herself to the ways of her household. He holds that she disposed of her husband’s goods without his knowledge not only lawfully but laudably, because it was not to gratify her own pride but for the necessary defence of a family otherwise inevitably ruined. On the difficult phrase in the oath he had already taken the view Ellicott argues for, that David was going to say unto me and decently turned it off.

Gill gives the tactic rather than the terrain, that she sent the present ahead because the sight of it would in great measure pacify David and prepare him to hear her patiently. On the oath he alone takes the words at face value, as a wish that God would give David’s enemies as much health and wealth as Nabal has, and much more.

debates.question: Was the present liberal or implausibly small?

positions.view: Ample, and the original request modest: out of three thousand sheep five could not have been missed
The versions found it too small — the Septuagint enlarges the grain measure and Ewald would read five hundred — but the text stands, the present being for David’s immediate followers

debates.question: Whom does the oath imprecate — David, or his enemies?

positions.view: David himself; the Hebrew is correct and the Syriac and Arabic reading of his servant David shows the difficulty felt
David was going to say unto me, and decently turned it off
Literally his enemies: a wish that God would give them as much health and wealth as Nabal has, and more

outliers.claim: Alone in grounding Abigail’s disposal of her husband’s goods in the doctrine of necessity rather than in her prudence or her household office.
Alone in refusing any mitigation of David’s oath, and in making the attempt to vindicate it itself an offence against truth.
Alone in reading the oath’s reference to David’s enemies literally rather than as a euphemism for David himself.

themes: Then Abigail made haste, and took two hundred loaves, and two bottles of wine
she said unto her servants, Go on before me; behold, I come after you. But she told not her husband Nabal
as she rode on the ass, that she came down by the covert of the hill
he hath requited me evil for good
So and more also do God unto the enemies of David, if I leave of all that pertain to him by the morning light any that pisseth against the wall

23.pericope_label: Abigail’s plea: the fool’s folly, the blood David is withheld from, and the bundle of life

schools.summary: Wesley marks the method of the speech: by absolutely submitting to mercy without any pretence of justifying what was done, and rather aggravating it, she works upon David’s generosity, and there is hardly a head of argument the greatest orator might use here that she does not manage to the best advantage. Her opening he glosses as a formal substitution, that Nabal’s sin be imputed to her and punished in her, who offers herself as a sacrifice to David’s indignation. Her prayer about his enemies he presses further than the others do: let them be forced to yield and implore thy pardon as Nabal now does by my mouth, and let the vengeance designed against this house fall rather on those whose inveterate malice deserves it more than a fool’s miscarriage. Clarke handles two clauses without apparatus. Of the evil not found in David he reads plain record, that David had committed no act of this kind hitherto; and of the bundle of life he takes the sense to be that the life shall be precious in the Lord’s sight, supported by him who is the Spring and Fountain of life, while the enemies are cast off as a stone from a sling, which he says betokens both force and violence.

Ellicott reads the obeisance as evidence of what Abigail believed about the man she knelt to, her tone betokening a consciousness that she addressed the anointed of Jehovah and future king, and notes that she deprecates his wrath by representing her husband not merely as bad but as scarcely responsible. On her central claim he follows the Speaker’s Commentary: since the oath affirms nothing, it should be rendered as true as that the Lord liveth, so true is it that the Lord hath withholden thee from blood-guiltiness; and so confident is she of doing the Lord’s work that before an armed band she speaks as though the danger were already past and David had real cause for thankfulness at being prevented from a wanton and wicked act. Of the prayer about his enemies he takes her to dismiss Nabal as too insignificant to consider, so that her wish is that the rest be equally harmless. He goes furthest on her foresight, holding that unconsciously she repeats words she may have heard in Samuel’s school by Ramah, thinking of the young captain before her as the future hero-king, while the unconscious prophetess never dreamed of that glorious and holy One in whose person, far down the stream of ages, the Eternal would make good her words. Keil and Delitzsch say she gives such clear expression to her firm belief in the divine election of David as king that her words almost amount to prophecy, and note that the evil not found in him means misfortune rather than wrong-doing, that thought arriving only later in the speech.

debates.question: What does the bundle of life promise?

positions.view: Primarily the safe preservation of the righteous on earth in the grace and fellowship of the Lord, with eternal life following for those the Lord will not let perish; the metaphor is from binding valuable things in a bundle against injury

One of the earliest definite expressions of belief in an eternal future in God’s presence — a favourite inscription on Jewish gravestones, with the Talmud hiding the souls of the righteous beneath God’s throne — and perhaps the original of the apostle’s picture of the souls of them that were slain
That the life shall be precious in the Lord’s sight, supported by him who is the Spring and Fountain of life

debates.question: What is the evil that has not been found in David?

positions.view: Misfortune, not wrong-doing; the thought of wrong-doing enters only later in the speech
Wrong-doing of this kind: David had committed no such act hitherto

outliers.claim: Alone in tracing Abigail’s language to the prophetic schools at Ramah and in extending her words past David to one far down the stream of ages.
Alone in reading her prayer about David’s enemies as a petition that they be brought to beg pardon as Nabal does, rather than merely as a wish that they prove harmless.

themes: Upon me, my lord, upon me let this iniquity be
the Lord hath withholden thee from coming to shed blood, and from avenging thyself with thine own hand
the soul of my lord shall be bound in the bundle of life with the Lord thy God
the souls of thine enemies, them shall he sling out, as out of the middle of a sling
evil hath not been found in thee all thy days

32.pericope_label: David blesses God and Abigail, renounces his oath, and sends her home in peace

schools.summary: Henry sets a proverb over the exchange, that a wise reprover upon an obedient ear is as an ear-ring of gold, and says never was such an admonition either better given or better taken, David acting on his own principle that if the righteous smite him it shall be a kindness. Most people think it enough to take a reproof patiently, he adds, but few will take it thankfully and commend the one who gives it; and Abigail did not rejoice more at having saved her husband and family from death than David did that she had saved him and his men from sin. He notices the order of the thanks: God first, for sending the check to a sinful way, since God is to be acknowledged in all the kindnesses our friends do us and whoever meets us with counsel or caution or seasonable reproof we must see God sending them; then Abigail, blessed be thy advice and blessed be thou. Of the danger Henry has David speak as of something barely escaped, since he was coming to shed blood, a sin he had a great horror of when in his right mind, and coming to avenge himself with his own hand, which would have been stepping into the throne of God, who has said that vengeance is his.

Gill puts the moment more plainly, that David heard her out and was overcome by her rhetoric and powerful arguments, and renders the word he blesses as her taste, her good sense, or, with the Targum, her discretion. Of the dismissal he notes that David took the present kindly for himself and his men, it being a gift fit for a prince.

Keil and Delitzsch summarise the reply in the same order Henry gives and spend their note on a single word, an imperfect carrying a perfect termination, which they take not for a copyist’s error but for an intensified form of the second person feminine. Ellicott reaches the doctrine that an oath to do evil is void by comparison rather than by rule. He notes that David, with his usual frank generosity, allows he was in the wrong in giving way to ungovernable passion and openly confesses that but for Abigail he would have carried out his purpose and stained his fair fame for ever; that his dark purpose had been to cut off root and branch the whole house of Nabal, the woman before him included; and that never had a more solemn vow been taken, yet before sunset he was convinced of its wickedness and deliberately broke it. Against that he sets two men who did not break theirs: Saul, who but for the people would have murdered his own son to fulfil the rash oath sworn at Michmash, and Jephthah, who ruthlessly carried out his wild and useless oath in the person of his daughter.

Wesley states the same doctrine as a rule: it plainly appears that oaths whereby men bind themselves to any sin are null and void, and as it was a sin to make them, so it is adding sin to sin to perform them. Of the dismissal he notes only that David showed his acceptance of her person by granting her request.

outliers.claim: Alone in testing the broken oath against Saul at Michmash and Jephthah, making David’s reversal a merit measured against two men who kept wicked vows.
Alone in treating the passage as a grammatical problem, defending an irregular verb form against the charge of being a copyist’s error.

themes: Blessed be the Lord God of Israel, which sent thee this day to meet me
blessed be thy advice, and blessed be thou, which hast kept me this day from coming to shed blood
except thou hadst hasted and come to meet me, surely there had not been left… any that pisseth against the wall
Go up in peace to thine house; see, I have hearkened to thy voice, and have accepted thy person

36.pericope_label: Nabal’s feast and death, David’s marriage to Abigail, and Michal given to Phalti

schools.summary: Henry counts Nabal thrice dead in this passage, beginning with dead drunk: he held a feast like a king’s though his guests were but his shearers, and it is very common for those most niggardly in any act of piety to be most profuse in gratifying a vain humour, a mite being grudged to God and his poor while gold is lavished to make a fair show in the flesh. He never thought he could bestow too little in charity, Henry adds, nor too much in luxury. Of Abigail’s silence he gives the reason and the maxim together: she told him nothing, for being drunk he was as incapable of hearing reason as of speaking it, and to advise men in drink is to cast pearls before swine.

Ellicott draws the contrast between husband and wife as a contrast of eras: the husband churlish and unyielding, a friend of Saul and of the old disorderly state of things, falling at last a victim to his own untamed passions, is an extreme though not uncommon example of the leading Israelites before Samuel, while Abigail represents the nobler spirit after Samuel’s influence had worked upon the land. On the death he lays out two possibilities, fear, or a furious burst of anger that his wife should have humiliated herself before a man he hated, and judges fear the more probable. Of the last verse he reads the giving away of Michal as a deliberate breach: the act was high-handed and showed a fixed determination to break utterly and for ever with David, Phalti being presumably a chieftain Saul wished to attract to his fortunes; and her story does not end there, since after Saul’s death David would consent to friendship with Abner only if the princess were taken from Phalti and restored. Keil and Delitzsch refuse the choice of causes and make it compound: not his anger at the loss, nor merely his alarm at a danger he did not believe over, but also his vexation that his wife should have made him humble himself so, for he was a hard and self-willed man; and ten days later the Lord ended his life by a second stroke.

Clarke makes the death pure terror: he was thunderstruck, so terrified at what he had escaped that the fear overcame his mind, he became insensible to all around him, and died in ten days. On the marriages he reasons that David had heard Saul married Michal to Phalti in order to cut off his pretensions to the throne, which justified him in taking Abigail or any other woman, it not being then unlawful to take several wives, and supposes that by the marriage David probably came into all Nabal’s property in Carmel and Maon. Of the second wife he reports the view of many that Ahinoam was his before Abigail, being always named first in the lists and the mother of his eldest son; and he notes the man is called Phaltiel elsewhere and that his town probably lay in Benjamin, so Saul likely chose him for being of his own tribe. Wesley gives the same cause as Clarke but in a figure: Nabal fainted through the horror of a mischief already past, as one who had galloped by night over a narrow plank laid on a broken bridge and, coming in the morning to review it, was struck dead with horror at the danger he had been in. He calls the blessing David pronounced over the news another instance of human infirmity, and warns that the proposal which follows was doubtless not made immediately upon Nabal’s death but some time after, such circumstances being commonly omitted in the sacred history, which gives only the heads and chief passages of things.

positions.view: Terror: he was thunderstruck at what he had escaped, became insensible, and died in ten days
Horror at a mischief already past, like a man who sees by daylight the broken bridge he crossed in the dark
Either fear or a furious burst of anger at his wife’s humiliating herself before a man he hated, with fear the more probable
A compound cause — not anger at the loss, nor merely alarm at a danger he did not believe over, but vexation that his wife had made him humble himself, he being hard and self-willed

outliers.claim: Alone in cautioning that the proposal to Abigail must have come well after the death, the sacred history giving only the heads and chief passages of things.
Alone in reckoning the material consequence, that the marriage probably brought David all of Nabal’s property in Carmel and Maon.
Alone in reading the disposal of Michal as deliberate dynastic policy whose sequel is her later recovery from Phalti.

themes: Nabal held a feast in his house, like the feast of a king… for he was very drunken
his heart died within him, and he became as a stone
the Lord smote Nabal, that he died
Blessed be the Lord, that hath pleaded the cause of my reproach from the hand of Nabal
But Saul had given Michal his daughter, David’s wife, to Phalti the son of Laish
